fetched_contents.text: Comparative analysis of constructed wetlands: The design and construction of the ecotechnology research facility in Langenreichenbach, Germany Introduction In many parts of the world, wastewater from individual dwellings and small settlements has historically been discharged into the environment with only coarse primary treatment in a septic tank or without any treatment at all, often posing a significant threat to public and environmental health (Gardner et al., 1997, Mara, 2003). In order to limit groundwater contamination and eutrophication of surface waters, regulations for the discharge of treated wastewater have become more stringent in recent years, making nutrient removal an increasingly common requirement for small and decentralized treatment systems. Given the increasing emphasis on reuse of treated effluent (particularly in the drier regions of the world), the fate of pathogens in decentralized treatment systems is also of concern. Owing to the variable wastewater flows and relatively remote locations typical of on-site and decentralized treatment systems, technologies must be robust and capable of operating with minimal maintenance or supervision. For these reasons, there is a growing awareness that technologies designed with natural processes and ecological principles in mind, or ecotechnologies such as treatment wetlands, are especially appropriate for decentralized applications (Sasse, 1998, Wallace and Knight, 2006, Hoffmann et al., 2011). Compared to conventional wastewater technologies, treatment wetlands are low-cost, relatively simple to operate, and can be constructed out of local materials. Recent research has also demonstrated that treatment wetlands are not only capable of meeting secondary treatment standards, but can also achieve high levels of total nitrogen removal through careful design and technology selection (Tanner et al., 2012). These aspects lend to the widespread implementation of treatment wetlands throughout the world. Subsurface oxygen limitation is one of the main rate limiting factors for traditional horizontal flow treatment wetland designs, especially when nitrification (and subsequent total nitrogen removal) is a treatment objective (Brix and Schierup, 1990). As a result, one of the biggest driving forces fuelling the evolution of treatment wetland technology has been the desire to increase subsurface oxygen availability (and thus, treatment performance). Design variants now span from completely passive systems (horizontal flow), to moderately engineered systems (unsaturated vertical flow systems with pulse loading) up to highly engineered or intensified systems (with increased pumping, water level fluctuation, or active aeration) (Fonder and Headley, 2010). Although technically classified as treatment wetlands, these various designs represent a broad spectrum of technologies. This technical diversity can be likened to that of the general term “activated sludge”, which encompasses a broad range of aerated suspended-growth technologies. Across the wetland technology gradient from passive to intensified systems, there are trade-offs between the system footprint and energy requirement. A decrease in required area typically comes at a cost of increased electricity consumption, and potentially more complex design and operational requirements. By virtue of being ecological technologies, treatment wetlands bridge the gap between “hard engineering” and natural science. Because of this, treatment wetland professionals are widely scattered amongst the various disciplines of engineering (agricultural, chemical, environmental, civil and mechanical) and natural sciences (biology, botany, chemistry, ecology, geology and microbiology) within universities, research institutes, non-profit organizations, and consulting engineering firms across the globe. The broad base of expertise among the professionals in this field makes highly synergistic and inter-disciplinary research efforts possible (and desirable). That said, the majority of treatment wetland research today is strongly delineated by geography, just as it has been in the past. Some of the geographical limitations can be attributed to local regulations, which sometimes dictate specific designs that are readily accepted by local authorities; as is the case in Austria (Österreichisches Normungsinstitut, 2005), Denmark (Brix and Arias, 2004), France (Macrophytes et Traitement des Eaux, 2005), Germany (Gesellschaft zur Förderung der Abwassertechnik, 1998), England (CIRIA, 1997, Wessex Water, 2006), and Spain (García and Corzo, 2008), among other countries. In such instances, there is more motivation (and often, more funding) to dig deeper into the mechanisms and science of the “locally designated” design as opposed to expanding research efforts across geographical boundaries (and thus, across different types of treatment wetlands). As a result, the treatment wetland discipline is often characterized by pockets of intense research based on the locally accepted design and/or basic discipline of the professionals (be it engineering or one of the sciences). Collaboration across these boundaries is not unknown, but it is not especially common. An interesting aspect about the advancement of treatment wetland technology is that new developments often come from practitioners and consultants working in the private sector. These individuals, who may not publish scientific papers very often (or at all), have developed variations of wetland technology through internal research and development efforts and lessons learned the hard way (mainly through trial and error at their own expense). Because economics and treatment efficiency are the main driving factors for any consulting engineer, these technology advances are typically quite pragmatic in nature and quickly implemented upon proof of concept. fetched_contents.text: Efficient removal of nitrogen from tidal flow constructed wetlands based on the in-situ zeolite regeneration: Measures and mechanisms Introduction According to the Chinese Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, sewage treatment rates were only 28 % in 2021. The Chinese government formulated policies to develop glorious villages that encouraged rural residents to integrate domestic sewage treatment and ecological courtyard construction [1]. However, because the density of the Chinese rural population was low and living was dispersed, it was critical to investigate a simple sewage treatment technology to operate and maintain [2]. Constructed wetlands (CWs) show two functions: sewage treatment and environmental beautification, which are regarded as the best options for rural sewage treatment. However, it is often used for the deep treatment of residential, industrial, and domestic wastewaters [3], [4]. For example, the vertical subsurface flow constructed wetlands (VFCWs) cause a higher removal effect on organic pollutants, nitrogen, and suspended solids. The wetland bed can be blocked due to the proliferation of microorganisms. Therefore, the sewage concentration of COD and NH4+-N flowing into the wetland should not be >200 mg·L−1 and 25 mg·L−1, respectively. The organic loading rate is 80–120 kgBOD5·(hm2·d)−1. The NH4+-N concentration in sewage has increased to 20–90 mg·L−1 since the diversion collection of gray and black water has not been achieved in most rural areas of China [5]. It is evident that the CWs has no advantage in treating the rural sewage. Tidal flow constructed wetlands (TFCWs) are one of the breakthroughs in CW research. It has significantly improved the capacity to treat NH4+-N [6], [7]. There are four steps in the TFCWs operating period: influent, flood, effluent, and drain. During the influent and flood period, NH4+-N is adsorbed, and its concentration in the liquid period of the TFCWs decreases. Negative pressure is generated during the effluent phase, and the air enters TFCWs by siphonage. Therefore, dissolved oxygen (DO) in TFCWs is sufficient and enough to oxidate NH4+-N into NOx−-N through nitrification. These processes achieve the in-situ filler regeneration of TFCWs. Then, organic matter is rapidly consumed by microorganisms during the next flood period, reducing oxygen concentration. Finally, denitrifying bacteria convert NOx−-N into N2. It is worth noting that although the tidal strategy improves the NH4+-N removal effect of the constructed wetland, it also inhibits its denitrification capacity. In recent years, some researchers have improved TFCWs’ denitrification capability through various operational strategies. Flood/drain time ratio [8], flood time [9], step feeds strategy [7], and multiple sub-cycle feeds strategy [10] are critical measures and have been investigated. However, they all need any complicated operatings or additional cost input and don’t balance nitrification and denitrification processes. Furthermore, tidal flow operations cause the stratification of adsorbed substances [11], [12], [13], which reduces the denitrification effect of TFCWs. Unfortunately, stratification has not been paid enough attention and research. The change in the influent mode may have the potential to improve TFCW nitrification and denitrification capacity by releasing the original pollutant treatment potential of TFCWs. A relevant study showed that the upflow influent had a greater capacity for denitrification than the downflow influent [14], but the downflow influent achieved a quick nitrification process [15]. Two-way influent (influent from the top and bottom layers) may be used to balance nitrification and denitrification processes and improve the nitrogen removal capacity of TFCWs. Nevertheless, there is no experimental demonstration and perfect theory on the relationship between the stratification of the adsorbed substances and nitrogen removal. Additionally, the mechanism of nitrogen removal enhanced by two-way influent is not clear enough and needs to be further investigated. This work aimed to 1) analyze the removal efficiencies of NH4+-N, COD, and NOx−-N in TFCWs, 2) investigate the reasons for the stratification of adsorbed substances, 3) establish the relationship between the stratification of the adsorbed substances and nitrogen removal, and 4) assess whether TFCWs with two-way influent facilitate nitrogen removal and clarify the removal mechanism. The results showed that (1) The ceramsite system’s filtration efficacy in treating wastewater is primarily driven by deep filtration processes. The distribution of water flow within the ceramsite wetland system is more homogenous than that observed in the blast furnace slag wetland system. Furthermore, the ceramsite system exhibits enhanced utilization of the primary bed area, the underlying drainage layer, and the catchment zone. (2) The blast furnace slag system possesses a smaller porosity and particle size distribution, which results in non-uniform flow rates and pressure distributions. Consequently, this system is prone to clogging, leading to a decline in both hydraulic performance and the overall functionality of the wetland. (3) The ceramsite system exhibits a lower occurrence of dead zones within the main bed compared to the blast furnace slag system, with a reduction of 12.58% and 27.93% in the dead zone percentages, respectively. This suggests that the ceramsite system outperforms the blast furnace slag system in terms of hydraulic efficiency, resistance to clogging, and contaminant removal efficacy. 1 Introduction Horizontal flow constructed wetland (HFCW) are widely used in the field of water pollution treatment because of their advantages, such as good treatment effects and low infrastructure and operation costs (House et al., 1999). However, clogging is common in HFCWs after a period of operation. Relevant statistics show that 50% of wetlands experience some extent of clogging within 5 years of operation (USEAP, 1993). Clogging causes uneven hydraulic distribution in the wetland system, reduces the porosity of the substrate, shortens the hydraulic retention time (HRT) of the system, affects the pollutant treatment efficiency, and, in severe cases, reduces the service life of the wetland (Nivala et al., 2012). The clogging problem of HFCWs has received attention in recent years, several studies have been reported to initially explore the clogging distribution patterns in HFCWs (Knowles et al., 2010; Petitjean et al., 2016), clogging extent monitoring (Morris et al., 2011; Hughes-Riley et al., 2016; Corbella et al., 2016), and two-dimensional models of clogging (Hua et al., 2010). The spatial and temporal distribution, as well as the flow field characteristics of clogged areas within artificial wetlands, have been investigated using Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) (Dai et al., 2024). Nonetheless, the flow field characteristics, the extent and location of dead zones, and the size of clogging volumes in wetland systems remain relatively underexplored, particularly in ceramic and blast furnace slag wetland systems. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is a product of the combination of recent fluid mechanics, numerical mathematics, and computer science that analyzes complex physical problems containing fluid flow and heat transfer through computer numerical calculation and image display, and finally can obtain the basic physical quantities such as velocity, pressure, temperature, and concentration in the flow field and a quantitative description to solve various practical problems (Persson et al., 1999; Fan et al., 2008). In recent years, CFD numerical simulation methods have also been applied to the study of artificial wetland flow fields, laying the foundation for the establishment of hydrodynamic models of constructed wetland as well as the simulation and analysis of flow patterns inside wetlands (Fan et al., 2008; Rengers et al., 2016). Rengers used CFD methods to study the hydrodynamic performance of constructed wetland systems, and the results showed that flow velocity, length, and interaction between flow rate and length had significant effects on the content of pollutants in the effluent; Jang used numerical simulation to determine the factors affecting the nitrate reduction process in aquifer heterogeneity (Rengers et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2017). Garcia mainly studied the effects of different constructed wetland sizes and substrates of different particle sizes on the hydraulics of horizontal flow constructed wetland and found that larger wetland aspect ratios and smaller particle sizes, as well as the filling form of the substrate and the location of the inlet and outlet, directly affected the dead zone and particle removal efficiency within the constructed wetland (Garcia et al., 2004; Kjellin et al., 2006; Choi and Park, 2013). Rajabzadeh et al. (2015) simulated the flow field and biokinetics in a vertical flow wetland using CFD. (2024) optimized the hydraulic performance of a bulkhead-style horizontal subsurface flow artificial wetland by utilizing CFD modeling. Similarly, Du et al. (2024) demonstrated that CFD models are a potent tool for the hydraulic characterization of surface flow constructed wetlands (SSF-CW) through their CFD modeling efforts. CIIMAR/CIMAR LA, Interdisciplinary Centre of Marine and Environmental Research, University of Porto, Matosinhos, Portugal * See more Article metrics View details Abstract Constructed wetland (CW) systems offer many advantages for wastewater treatment in urban areas and are increasingly seen as sustainable solutions. However, their pollutant removal capacity can vary significantly, influenced by weather conditions and the specific plant species used. This paper presents a long-term study conducted on two pilot-scale horizontal subsurface flow (HSSF) CWs located in two different towns of Sicily (Italy). The main aims were to compare the pollutant removal efficiency (RE) of two HSSF CWs treating urban wastewater and to assess the effect of treated wastewater (TWW) reuse on bermudagrass [Cynodon dactylon (L.) Pers.] traits and soil characteristics. The two CWs had comparable surface areas and were each planted with a different species, resulting in monoculture systems. Two experimental fields of bermudagrass were set up, one for each HSSF CW. The effects of 3 years and two sources of irrigation water [TWW and freshwater (FW) as control] were assessed using a split-plot design for two-factor experiments. Results highlight that removal efficiencies up to 83% were achieved for an inlet of 55 ± 14 mg COD L−1, 81% for an inlet of 31 ± 5 mg BOD5 L−1, 66% for an inlet of 20.6 ± 3.5 mg total nitrogen L−1, and 50% for an inlet of 7.9 ± 0.8 mg total phosphorus L−1. Both CW systems demonstrated effective long-term performance in the removal of physico-chemical and microbiological contaminants. Bermudagrass had higher above-ground biomass production (1,358.74 kg ha−1) in TWW-irrigated plots than those plots irrigated with FW (1,005.98 kg ha−1), on average. The highest biomass yields were recorded during the second and third years of the study. Visual turf quality ratings were consistently similar across years and irrigation treatments. No significant variations in soil pH were observed between FW- and TWW-irrigated soils. However, soils irrigated with TWW showed higher salinity, organic matter, macronutrients, and sodium levels, on average. 1 Introduction Constructed wetland (CW) systems are engineered systems designed for wastewater (WW) treatment and reuse, and since the last century they have been increasingly recognized to play a strategic role in delivering a range of ecosystem services (Wu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021; Agaton and Guila, 2023). They are designed to remove contaminants from various types of wastewaters in a controlled environment by replicating the natural processes that occur in wetlands (Vymazal, 2014; Hassan et al., 2021; Gebru and Werkneh, 2024; Addo-Bankas et al., 2024). Microorganisms, plants, and substrates are key components of CWs, and their synergistic interaction enables these systems to achieve higher treatment efficiency compared to natural wetlands (Ji et al., 2022; Kushwaha et al., 2024). Treated wastewater (TWW) and plant biomass are the primary outputs of CWs, and their use can greatly increase the multi-functionality of these systems (Masi et al., 2017; Takavakoglou et al., 2022). In particular, in the semi-arid environment, TWW is an effective alternative water supply, and its use forms one of the most promising strategies for sustainable water management, due to its potential environmental benefits for soil health and water quality (Stefanakis, 2019; Franci Gonçalves et al., 2021; Licata et al., 2019; de Campos and Soto, 2024)…

Oxygen transfer is central to nitrogen removal in wetlands because nitrification and denitrification depend on different redox conditions. In conventional wetlands, oxygen availability often limits nitrification and can suppress denitrification, which typically requires anaerobic conditions. The cited evidence states that traditional horizontal flow treatment wetlands face subsurface oxygen limitation, especially when nitrification is a treatment objective, and that increasing subsurface oxygen availability has been a major driver of wetland technology evolution [N1-F1]. It also notes that oxygen transfer and consumption mechanisms in treatment wetlands are complex and include physical, chemical, and biological processes [N2-R3]. This establishes oxygen transfer as a performance bottleneck rather than an incidental factor.

Tidal flow wetlands affect dissolved oxygen availability and redox conditions through their alternating flooding and draining phases. The evidence from the tidal flow constructed wetland overview explicitly says tidal operation creates an anaerobic/aerobic alternating environment through tidal operation, greatly enhancing oxygen supply [N1-R4]. Another source describes tidal flow wetlands as having a flooding phase and a draining phase, with the draining phase generating negative pressure and allowing air to enter by siphonage, which replenishes dissolved oxygen (DO) [N3-F2]. This means tidal flow does not simply maintain a steady aerobic state; it actively cycles between oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions, which is important for nitrogen cycling.

The implications for nitrogen removal efficiency and stoichiometry are clear. Nitrification is an aerobic process, so higher oxygen availability generally supports it [N1-F1]. Denitrification, by contrast, is anaerobic and requires reduced oxygen or even anoxic conditions. The evidence shows that tidal flow can suppress denitrification capacity in some studies, because stratification of adsorbed substances reduces denitrification effect [N3-F2]. However, tidal flow can also enhance nitrification by improving DO supply and creating a more dynamic oxygen regime. The cited review on nitrogen removal processes and mechanisms notes that tidal flow wetlands operate through a flooding phase (FP) and draining phase (DP), which implies a structured alternation of conditions suitable for both nitrification and denitrification [N3-R1]. The evidence also suggests that the balance between nitrification and denitrification can be mediated by operational strategies such as flood/drain time ratio, step feeds, and multiple sub-cycle feeds [N3-F2]. This indicates that tidal flow wetlands do not inherently favor one pathway over the other; instead, their performance depends on how the oxygen/redox cycle is managed and whether the system can sustain the right conditions for both processes.

Overall, oxygen transfer in wetlands is not just a supply issue. It shapes the overall nitrogen removal stoichiometry by enabling nitrification when oxygen is available and supporting denitrification when it is not. In tidal flow wetlands, the alternating tidal regime improves oxygen supply and creates a more favorable environment for nitrogen cycling overall, but it can also create trade-offs if denitrification is constrained by stratification or insufficient anaerobic periods [N3-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a nuanced view: tidal flow enhances nitrogen removal through improved oxygen transfer and redox cycling, but the efficiency depends on how well the system balances aerobic nitrification with anaerobic denitrification [N1-F1][N1-R4][N3-F2].

Nitrogen removal mechanisms in tidal flow wetlands are distinct from conventional wetlands because tidal operation creates an alternating aerobic-anaerobic environment and changes microbial community dynamics. The evidence directly states that tidal flow constructed wetlands (TFCWs) create an anaerobic/aerobic alternating environment through tidal operation, greatly enhancing oxygen supply [N1-R4]. It also notes that tidal flow wetlands operate through a flooding phase (FP) and a draining phase (DP), which is a key structural feature of their nitrogen removal process [N3-R1]. This alternating regime is central to nitrogen cycling, as nitrification occurs under aerobic conditions and denitrification under anaerobic or anoxic conditions.

The evidence shows that tidal flow wetlands can favor nitrification more strongly than conventional wetlands. In the TFCW study, during the influent and flood phase, NH4+-N is adsorbed, and during the effluent phase, negative pressure allows air to enter the system by siphonage, replenishing dissolved oxygen and enabling nitrification to oxidize NH4+-N into NOx−-N [N3-F2]. The same study also notes that after 30 days, zeolite adsorption becomes saturated and biofilm growth leads to a reaction equilibrium state, which suggests that nitrification is supported by both physical adsorption and biological oxidation [N3-F2]. This indicates that tidal flow wetlands are not merely passive adsorbers; they actively support aerobic nitrogen transformation.

Denitrification is also part of the nitrogen removal pathway, but the evidence suggests that tidal flow can inhibit it in some cases. The cited study states that tidal flow operations cause the stratification of adsorbed substances, which reduces the denitrification effect of TFCWs [N3-F2]. This stratification likely disrupts microbial access to substrate and creates uneven oxygen/redox conditions that weaken anaerobic denitrification. The same source also says that although tidal strategy improves NH4+-N removal, it also inhibits denitrification capacity, and that operational strategies such as flood/drain time ratio, flood time, step feeds, and multiple sub-cycle feeds have been investigated to improve denitrification [N3-F2]. This indicates that tidal flow wetlands can support denitrification, but the process is sensitive to operational design and can be limited under standard tidal regimes.

Microbial community dynamics differ under tidal conditions because the alternating aerobic-anaerobic environment selects for different microbial populations. The evidence does not provide a direct microbial community profile, but it does emphasize that the nitrogen removal process involves both in-situ zeolite regeneration and biofilm growth [N3-F2]. This implies that microbial communities are important for sustaining the nitrogen removal pathway, especially after adsorption capacity is exhausted and biofilm-mediated processes take over. The study further notes that the mechanism of nitrogen removal enhanced by two-way influent is not yet fully clear and needs further investigation [N3-F2], suggesting that microbial dynamics are still under-researched under tidal conditions. The broader evidence also shows that constructed wetlands depend on synergistic interactions among microorganisms, plants, and substrates [N1-F1], so tidal flow likely modifies these interactions by changing the hydraulic and redox regime.

Limitations and trade-offs are important. The evidence explicitly states that tidal flow can inhibit denitrification capacity and cause stratification of adsorbed substances [N3-F2]. It also notes that some operational strategies are needed to improve denitrification, but they often require additional costs or complicated operations [N3-F2]. Furthermore, the cited review indicates that the relationship between adsorbed substance stratification and nitrogen removal remains underexplored, and the mechanism of two-way influent is not yet fully understood [N3-F2]. This suggests that tidal flow wetlands can enhance nitrogen removal, but their performance is not automatic; they require careful design to balance nitrification and denitrification, avoid stratification, and maintain microbial functionality [N3-F2][N1-F1].

In summary, tidal flow wetlands favor aerobic nitrification and support denitrification, but their nitrogen removal efficiency depends on operational design. They create a dynamic microbial environment shaped by alternating aerobic and anaerobic conditions, which can enhance nitrogen removal overall, yet they also carry trade-offs such as inhibited denitrification and the need for additional operational strategies [N1-R4][N3-R1][N3-F2].

Tidal flow wetlands enhance pollutant removal relative to conventional wetlands primarily through differences in hydraulic residence time, mixing patterns, and the resulting exposure of pollutants to treatment processes. The evidence shows that tidal flow wetlands operate through a flooding phase and a draining phase, creating a dynamic hydraulic regime [N3-R1]. This alternating operation increases hydraulic mixing and can shorten effective hydraulic residence time by allowing water to move through the system more frequently than in conventional horizontal flow systems [N1-F1]. The comparative analysis of constructed wetlands notes that conventional systems can suffer from subsurface oxygen limitation and uneven hydraulic distribution, whereas intensified systems such as tidal flow wetlands aim to improve oxygen availability and treatment performance [N1-F1]. This suggests that tidal flow improves mixing and reduces the risk of hydraulic short-circuiting or uneven residence time.

The evidence also supports the idea that tidal flow increases contact between pollutants and treatment mechanisms. In the tidal flow constructed wetland overview, the system is described as creating an anaerobic/aerobic alternating environment that greatly enhances oxygen supply [N1-R4]. The same source explains that during the effluent phase, negative pressure allows air to enter the system by siphonage, replenishing dissolved oxygen and supporting nitrification [N3-F2]. This means that tidal flow can improve oxygen transfer and create more favorable conditions for pollutant transformation, particularly nitrogen removal. It also implies that pollutants are exposed to a more variable and often more effective treatment regime than in steady-state conventional systems.

For suspended solids, BOD, TSS, and other common pollutants, the evidence is mixed but generally supportive of improved or comparable performance. The cited long-term study on two pilot-scale horizontal subsurface flow constructed wetlands reports removal efficiencies up to 83% for COD, 81% for BOD5, 66% for total nitrogen, and 50% for total phosphorus [N5-F4]. This shows that conventional wetlands can achieve substantial removal of common pollutants, but it does not directly compare tidal flow with conventional wetlands. However, the broader evidence on tidal flow wetlands indicates that they can remove BOD, TSS, and nitrogen effectively, with one study reporting good treatment performances for BOD, TSS, and nitrogen removal as well as phosphorus [N6-R3]. Another study on tidal flow wetlands says the tidal flow regime boosts nitrogen removal via specialized microbial communities and reports over 90% removal for some compounds in a pilot constructed wetland [N6-R5]. These findings suggest that tidal flow wetlands can match or exceed conventional wetlands for many pollutants, especially when design and operational conditions are optimized.

Evidence for improved or comparable performance across different studies is also present. The comparative study of 15 pilot-scale conventional and tidal flow wetlands reports a systematic assessment of treatment efficacy for CBOD5, TSS, and other parameters, which is directly relevant to the question [N6-R1]. The evidence also states that the study compares conventional and tidal flow wetlands, indicating that it can provide a direct performance benchmark [N6-R1]. The long-term study on two constructed wetlands reports consistent removal efficiencies across different hydraulic loading rates and retention times [N5-F4], which reinforces the idea that conventional wetlands can be reliable, but tidal flow wetlands may offer advantages in hydraulic and mixing performance. The evidence further notes that tidal flow wetlands can improve nitrification and reduce stratification effects, while still facing trade-offs such as inhibited denitrification under standard operation [N3-F2]. This indicates that performance improvements are not universal; they depend on pollutant class, hydraulic design, and operational conditions.

Overall, tidal flow wetlands enhance pollutant removal relative to conventional wetlands by improving hydraulic mixing, reducing residence-time inequality, and creating more favorable oxygen/redox conditions. For suspended solids, BOD, TSS, and nitrogen, the evidence supports improved or comparable performance, with some studies showing very high removal efficiencies [N5-F4][N6-R3][N6-R5]. However, the evidence also shows that conventional wetlands remain advantageous in some respects, particularly when the goal is consistent, steady-state treatment and when operational complexity is limited [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The strongest conclusion is therefore that tidal flow wetlands can outperform conventional wetlands in terms of hydraulic efficiency and nitrogen removal, especially when the system is designed to balance aerobic and anaerobic conditions, but performance depends on pollutant type and operational management [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F4][N6-R1].

Tidal flow wetlands outperform conventional wetlands in several ways, but their relative advantage depends on pollutant class and operational conditions. The strongest evidence is that tidal flow improves hydraulic mixing, reduces hydraulic residence-time inequality, and creates an alternating aerobic/anaerobic environment that can enhance oxygen supply and nitrogen removal [N1-F1][N1-R4][N3-R1]. The comparative evidence also shows that tidal flow wetlands can achieve substantial removal of common pollutants such as BOD, TSS, and nitrogen, with some studies reporting removal efficiencies exceeding 83% for COD, 81% for BOD5, 66% for total nitrogen, and 50% for total phosphorus in conventional systems [N5-F4]. For tidal flow wetlands, the evidence specifically notes good treatment performances for BOD, TSS, and nitrogen removal as well as phosphorus [N6-R3], and one pilot study reports over 90% removal for some compounds [N6-R5]. This suggests tidal flow can match or exceed conventional wetlands for many pollutants, especially when the system is designed to optimize hydraulic and oxygen conditions.

Tidal flow wetlands outperform conventional wetlands most clearly where nitrogen removal is the target. The evidence shows that tidal operation supports nitrification by improving dissolved oxygen availability, while the alternating flooding and draining phases create conditions suitable for both aerobic and anaerobic nitrogen cycling [N1-F1][N1-R4][N3-R1]. The specific tidal flow study explains that during the effluent phase, negative pressure allows air to enter the system by siphonage, replenishing dissolved oxygen and supporting nitrification [N3-F2]. This is a key advantage because conventional horizontal flow wetlands often suffer from subsurface oxygen limitation, which can restrict nitrification and overall nitrogen removal [N1-F1]. Tidal flow also boosts nitrogen removal via specialized microbial communities, according to one pilot study [N6-R5]. However, tidal flow can also inhibit denitrification capacity under standard operation because of adsorbed-substance stratification [N3-F2]. This means tidal wetlands can be superior for nitrification and overall nitrogen cycling, but their denitrification performance is sensitive to design and operation.

Conventional wetlands remain advantageous where steady-state operation and simplicity are priorities. The comparative analysis notes that conventional systems are low-cost, relatively simple to operate, and can be constructed from local materials, while intensified systems such as tidal flow wetlands require more complex design and operational requirements [N1-F1]. The long-term study on conventional horizontal subsurface flow wetlands reports consistent removal efficiencies across different hydraulic loading rates and retention times [N5-F4], which indicates reliability under routine conditions. The evidence also emphasizes that conventional wetlands can meet secondary treatment standards and achieve high total nitrogen removal through careful design [N1-F1]. Tidal flow constructed wetlands enhance pollutant removal compared to conventional wetlands by improving hydraulic mixing, creating a more dynamic treatment regime, and optimizing conditions for nitrogen cycling. The branch reports consistently point to a key distinction: tidal flow creates an alternating aerobic/anaerobic environment that improves oxygen supply and supports both nitrification and denitrification, while conventional wetlands often suffer from subsurface oxygen limitation and uneven hydraulic distribution [N1-F1][N1-R4][N3-F2]. This makes tidal flow wetlands especially attractive for nitrogen removal, but also means their performance depends on how well the system balances aerobic and anaerobic conditions [N1-F1][N3-F2].

### 1) How tidal flow wetlands enhance pollutant removal

Tidal flow wetlands enhance pollutant removal primarily through differences in hydraulic residence time and mixing patterns. The evidence shows that tidal flow creates a dynamic regime with alternating flooding and draining phases, which reduces hydraulic inequality and increases mixing [N3-R1][N1-F1]. This is important because uneven residence time can reduce the effectiveness of conventional horizontal flow systems, where short-circuiting and poor hydraulic distribution are common problems [N1-F1]. The branch report on conventional wetlands notes that subsurface oxygen limitation is one of the main rate-limiting factors for traditional designs, especially when nitrification is a treatment objective [N1-F1]. Tidal flow addresses this by improving oxygen availability and creating a more favorable hydraulic environment [N1-R4].

For suspended solids, BOD, TSS, and other common pollutants, the evidence supports improved or comparable performance across studies. The long-term study on two pilot-scale horizontal subsurface flow constructed wetlands reports removal efficiencies up to 83% for COD, 81% for BOD5, 66% for total nitrogen, and 50% for total phosphorus [N5-F4]. The comparative evidence on tidal flow wetlands is similarly encouraging: one study reports good treatment performances for BOD, TSS, and nitrogen removal as well as phosphorus [N6-R3], and a pilot tidal flow wetland reports over 90% removal for some compounds [N6-R5]. This suggests tidal flow can match or exceed conventional wetlands for many pollutants, especially when design and operational conditions are optimized [N6-R1][N6-R5].

### 2) Role of oxygen transfer in nitrogen removal

Oxygen transfer is central to nitrogen removal in wetlands because nitrification and denitrification depend on different redox conditions. In conventional wetlands, oxygen availability often limits nitrification, and denitrification typically requires anaerobic or anoxic conditions [N1-F1]. The evidence on oxygen transfer and consumption in treatment wetlands also emphasizes that these mechanisms are complex and include physical, chemical, and biological processes [N2-R3]. This means oxygen transfer is not just a supply issue; it shapes the overall nitrogen removal stoichiometry [N2-R3].

Tidal flow affects dissolved oxygen availability and redox conditions through its alternating tidal regime. The evidence states that tidal flow created by tidal operation creates an anaerobic/aerobic alternating environment, greatly enhancing oxygen supply [N1-R4]. In one tidal flow wetland study, during the effluent phase, negative pressure allows air to enter the system by siphonage, replenishing dissolved oxygen and supporting nitrification [N3-F2]. This means tidal flow does not simply maintain a steady aerobic state; it actively cycles between oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions, which is important for nitrogen cycling [N1-R4][N3-F2].

The implications for nitrogen removal efficiency and stoichiometry are clear. Nitrification is an aerobic process, so higher oxygen availability generally supports it [N1-F1]. Denitrification is anaerobic and requires reduced oxygen or even anoxic conditions [N1-F1]. The evidence shows that tidal flow can improve nitrification by enhancing oxygen supply, but it can also inhibit denitrification capacity under standard operation because of adsorbed-substance stratification [N3-F2]. This indicates that tidal flow can support both pathways, but the efficiency depends on how well the system balances aerobic nitrification with anaerobic denitrification [N1-F1][N3-F2].

### 3) Nitrogen removal mechanisms specific to tidal flow wetlands

Nitrogen removal mechanisms in tidal flow wetlands are distinct from conventional wetlands because tidal operation creates an alternating aerobic-anaerobic environment and changes microbial community dynamics. The evidence shows that tidal flow wetlands operate through a flooding phase (FP) and a draining phase (DP), which is a key structural feature of their nitrogen removal process [N3-R1]. This alternating regime is central to nitrogen cycling because nitrification occurs under aerobic conditions and denitrification under anaerobic or anoxic conditions [N1-F1][N1-R4].

Tidal flow can favor nitrification more strongly than conventional wetlands. In the tidal flow constructed wetland study, NH4+-N is adsorbed during the influent and flood phase, and during the effluent phase, negative pressure allows air to enter the system by siphonage, replenishing dissolved oxygen and enabling nitrification to oxidize NH4+-N into NOx−-N [N3-F2]. The same study notes that after 30 days, zeolite adsorption becomes saturated and biofilm growth leads to a reaction equilibrium state, suggesting that nitrification is supported by both physical adsorption and biological oxidation [N3-F2]. This indicates that tidal flow wetlands are not merely passive adsorbers; they actively support aerobic nitrogen transformation.

Denitrification is also part of the nitrogen removal pathway, but the evidence suggests that tidal flow can inhibit it in some cases. The cited study states that tidal flow operations cause the stratification of adsorbed substances, which reduces the denitrification effect of TFCWs [N3-F2]. This stratification likely disrupts microbial access to substrate and creates uneven oxygen/redox conditions that weaken anaerobic denitrification. The same source also says that although tidal strategy improves NH4+-N removal, it also inhibits denitrification capacity, and that operational strategies such as flood/drain time ratio, flood time, step feeds, and multiple sub-cycle feeds have been investigated to improve denitrification [N3-F2]. This indicates that tidal flow wetlands can support denitrification, but the process is sensitive to operational design and can be limited under standard tidal regimes [N3-F2].

Microbial community dynamics differ under tidal conditions because the alternating aerobic-anaerobic environment selects for different microbial populations. The evidence does not provide a direct microbial community profile, but it does emphasize that the nitrogen removal process involves both in-situ zeolite regeneration and biofilm growth [N3-F2]. This implies that microbial communities are important for sustaining the nitrogen removal pathway, especially after adsorption capacity is exhausted and biofilm-mediated processes take over. The study further notes that the mechanism of nitrogen removal enhanced by two-way influent is not yet fully clear and needs further investigation [N3-F2], suggesting that microbial dynamics are still under-researched under tidal conditions. The broader evidence also shows that constructed wetlands depend on synergistic interactions among microorganisms, plants, and substrates [N1-F1], so tidal flow likely modifies these interactions by changing the hydraulic and redox regime.

### 4) Limitations and trade-offs in nitrogen removal under tidal operation

The branch reports make clear that tidal flow wetlands are not a universal solution. They can inhibit denitrification capacity under standard operation because of adsorbed-substance stratification [N3-F2]. They can also create trade-offs between nitrification and denitrification, requiring operational strategies such as flood/drain time ratio, step feeds, and multiple sub-cycle feeds to improve denitrification [N3-F2]. The synthesis of comparative performance across pollutant classes and operational conditions shows that tidal flow wetlands outperform conventional wetlands in several ways, but their relative advantage depends on pollutant class and operational conditions.
